abstract.p: Groundwater in Egypt’s Siwa Oasis exhibits extreme hardness (total ≈ 3312.6 mg/L as CaCO3; Mg2+ ≈ 609.5 mg/L, Ca2+ ≈ 325.4 mg/L), far above guideline values and problematic for health and infrastructure. We report a sustainable softening approach using magnesium-silicate zeolite (Mg.ZA) synthesized from natural talc via alkali fusion (550 °C, 5 h) and mild hydrothermal conversion, producing LTA-type crystallinity with mesoporosity and high surface area (187 m2/g). Performance was evaluated under batch and fixed-bed (continuous-flow) conditions and interpreted with statistical-physics modeling. In batch at pH 7, Mg.ZA achieved 268.8 mg/g (Ca2+) and 206.9 mg/g (Mg2+), following pseudo-first-order kinetics and Langmuir isotherms, indicating physisorption-dominated, near-monolayer uptake. In fixed-bed tests with synthetic and real Siwa groundwater (flow 5 mL/min; pH ≈ 7; bed depth 1–3 cm), increasing bed depth to 3 cm extended breakthrough and raised dynamic capacities to ~ 279.6 mg/g (Ca2+) and ~ 227.8 mg/g (Mg2+); breakthrough and saturation were defined at 10% and 95%, respectively. Field relevance was demonstrated by treating real Siwa groundwater, reducing Ca2+/Mg2+ to acceptable levels across reuse cycles and confirming regenerability. The statistical-physics analysis quantified multi-ionic site occupancy (n > 2) and Qsat consistent with experiments (~ 269 mg/g Ca2+; ~207 mg/g Mg2+), with low adsorption energies (ΔE < 8 kJ/mol) supporting reversible, multilayer physisorption. Collectively, talc-derived Mg.ZA offers a cost-effective, eco-friendly, and scalable adsorbent capable of softening high-hardness groundwater under realistic conditions, supporting decentralized treatment in arid, resource-limited regions.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The infiltration of hazardous substances into water sources poses a critical threat to both ecological stability and public health, compromising the long-term viability of natural ecosystems and the wellbeing of human populations1–3. Groundwater, in particular, serves as a primary and often indispensable source of freshwater for drinking and urban consumption across the globe4,5. However, anthropogenic and natural activities, such as quarrying operations and intensive agricultural practices, facilitate the leaching of chemical elements from geological formations—rocks, soils, and minerals—leading to the degradation of water quality through elevated hardness levels6,7. Water hardness is predominantly attributed to the excessive concentrations of divalent calcium (Ca2+) and magnesium (Mg2+) ions, especially when levels exceed 60 mg/L8,9. In light of associated health and technical concerns, the World Health Organization has advised maintaining Ca2+ and Mg2+ concentrations in potable water below 75 mg/L and 50 mg/L, respectively10–12. Elevated hardness has been linked to a broad spectrum of adverse impacts spanning environmental, health, and economic domains. Technologically, the accumulation of mineral scale within pipelines and heating systems leads to efficiency losses and mechanical malfunctions. In particular, carbonate layer deposits exceeding 1 mm in thickness can escalate energy usage by approximately 12% while simultaneously diminishing operational efficiency13,14.

From a health perspective, prolonged exposure to high levels of water hardness has been associated with various medical conditions15. These include, but are not limited to, diarrheal illnesses, dermatitis, cardiovascular complications, cerebrovascular mortality, pancreatic and Alzheimer’s diseases, diabetes, kidney stones, digestive discomfort, constipation, reproductive disorders, central nervous system malformations, and decreased bone mineral density15,16. Egypt has been notably affected by this issue, with regions such as the Siwa Oasis experiencing persistent problems related to excessive water hardness17. Given these multifaceted consequences, the development and implementation of effective water-softening strategies is of paramount importance. Technologies such as chemical precipitation, coagulation, ion exchange, nanofiltration, adsorption, membrane separation, solvent extraction, and flocculation have been extensively researched and applied to remove Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions from water sources17–20.

Among these methods, adsorbent materials—particularly those derived from natural resources or synthetic silicate structures—have shown considerable promise in capturing divalent metal ions due to their high surface reactivity and ion exchange capacity21,22. Zeolite-based adsorbents, fabricated either from chemical precursors or naturally occurring resources, have emerged as versatile and economically viable candidates for water treatment applications23,24. These materials exhibit desirable attributes such as high porosity, large specific surface areas, structural stability, non-toxicity, and tunable physicochemical properties25–27. Zeolites are crystalline microporous aluminosilicates consisting of interconnected tetrahedral units of SiO₄ and AlO₄, forming a robust three-dimensional framework. This structure generates a system of cavities and channels, hosting a range of mobile alkali and alkaline earth metal cations, which are crucial to the ion exchange process28–31. Among the most widely studied synthetic zeolites are zeolite-A, zeolite-X, zeolite-Y, zeolite-P, cancrinite, and sodalite25,32–34.

The performance of synthesized zeolites is significantly influenced by the nature of the raw materials and the specific synthesis parameters employed. Factors such as crystallinity, surface area, pore size, and adsorption selectivity are directly governed by these variables27,35. Most current research has concentrated on the synthesis of zeolites from conventional aluminosilicate sources—primarily kaolinite and similar clay minerals—while relatively few studies have explored alternative phyllosilicate precursors with diverse chemical compositions, particularly magnesium-rich minerals such as talc36. Talc, a naturally abundant phyllosilicate mineral with the chemical composition Mg3(Si₄O₁₀)(OH)2, possesses a layered structure characterized by a TOT configuration—where a central brucite-like octahedral sheet is flanked by two tetrahedral silica sheets37,38. It is structurally monoclinic and exhibits properties including high surface area, low cost, extensive availability, and a balanced Si/Mg ratio, making it a promising precursor for the development of magnesium silicate zeolitic materials38–41. The previous investigation demonstrate successful synthesis of zeolite from talc and its application in the removal of heavy metals demonstrate significant efficiency38–41.

In this context, the present work introduces a novel and sustainable synthesis pathway for producing magnesium-rich zeolite-A (Mg.ZA) directly from natural talc, marking a significant departure from traditional aluminosilicate-based zeolite syntheses. Unlike common precursors such as kaolin, fly ash, or metakaolinite, talc provides a unique silica–magnesia framework that enables the formation of a distinct LTA-type zeolite with high crystallinity, large surface area, and mixed micro–mesoporosity. This transformation—achieved via a controlled alkali-fusion and mild hydrothermal process—represents the first comprehensive demonstration of zeolitization of natural talc for water-softening applications.

Scientifically, the study is pioneering in its integration of statistical-physics modeling with both batch and fixed-bed adsorption experiments, enabling quantitative interpretation of steric (site occupancy, saturation capacity) and energetic (adsorption energy, enthalpy, entropy) parameters. Practically, it is the first field-validated evaluation of talc-derived zeolite for real groundwater purification, tested under the challenging conditions of the Siwa Oasis, where extreme hardness and Mg-rich chemistry prevail. Collectively, this research establishes a new class of magnesium-silicate zeolitic adsorbents derived from abundant natural minerals—combining scientific innovation, environmental sustainability, and practical scalability. The developed Mg.ZA material demonstrates strong selectivity and reusability for Ca2+ and Mg2+ removal, offering a low-cost, green alternative for decentralized water treatment in arid and resource-limited regions.

sec.title: Site description and hydrology
sec.p: Situated in the northern sector of Egypt’s Western Desert, the Siwa Oasis spans an approximate area of 1,100 square kilometers and is located nearly 320 km inland from the Mediterranean coastline. This remote settlement supports a local population estimated at 23,000 inhabitants (Fig. 1)17,42. The region’s economy is predominantly sustained by agricultural activities, with particular emphasis on the cultivation of date palms, olive production, and the farming of a variety of fruits and vegetables. In addition to agriculture, Siwa hosts small-scale industrial operations, such as mineral water bottling and olive oil processing, which play a vital role in reinforcing the economic resilience of the area42,43. Climatically, the oasis is classified as hyper-arid, receiving minimal precipitation—averaging just 10 mm annually. The region also experiences high evaporation rates, which can peak at approximately 16.8 mm per day during the summer season and drop to around 5.4 mm per day in winter. These severe environmental conditions, compounded by the oasis’s geographic seclusion and scarce water availability, present significant obstacles to both human livelihood and economic productivity44,45.

The geological structure of Siwa Oasis is marked by a heterogeneous assemblage of hydrostratigraphic units. Surface formations are dominated by Quaternary deposits, which manifest as sand dunes and salt flats and extend into shallow subsurface layers. Beneath these, the Tertiary Carbonate Aquifer (TCA), comprising sedimentary formations from the Miocene and Eocene epochs, includes layers of limestone and dolomite interbedded with minor sequences of shale and clay. Further below, the subsurface geology includes ancient Paleozoic basement rocks and Mesozoic strata such as the Lower Cretaceous Nubian Sandstone and Upper Cretaceous shale, adding to the area’s complex stratigraphic profile46.

Groundwater in Siwa is primarily extracted from two major aquifers systems: the relatively shallow TCA and the deeper Nubian Sandstone Aquifer System (NSSS). The Miocene segment of the TCA is chiefly utilized to meet agricultural and domestic needs, while the NSSS serves as a critical source for both irrigation and potable water supplies (Fig. 1)47. However, various environmental problems have emerged, particularly soil salinization and waterlogging, which are most acute in regions adjacent to salt lakes such as Zeitoun in the east, Aghormi and Siwa in the central area, and Maraqi in the west. These issues underscore the urgent need for the development and implementation of sustainable water management practices45,47,48. Hydraulic head data collected from 27 monitoring wells reveal that groundwater in the NSSS predominantly flows along southeast-to-northwest (SE-NW) and southwest-to-northeast trajectories. Nevertheless, unsustainable groundwater abstraction—mainly driven by intensive agricultural use—has led to the formation of a pronounced cone of depression in the central part of the oasis. This phenomenon highlights the pressing necessity to regulate groundwater withdrawal in order to maintain a balance between agricultural productivity and the conservation of environmental resources47.

sec.title: Materials
sec.p: The raw talc utilized in this study was sourced from the Bir Meseh deposit in Egypt’s Eastern Desert, situated south of Shalatin. This material was supplied by El-Nasr Mining Company, headquartered in Cairo, Egypt. The chemical composition of the talc sample, determined through standard analytical techniques, revealed the following constituent oxides: 46.35% SiO2, 9.54% CaO, 25.53% MgO, 0.12% SO3, 3.86% Al2O3, 2.16% Fe2O3, 0.02% K2O, 0.13% P2O5, 0.28% TiO2, 0.18% Na2O, along with a loss on ignition (L.O.I.) of 11.83%. Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) pellets, with a purity of 97%, were procured from the local distributor of Sigma-Aldrich (Cairo, Egypt) and employed as the alkaline activator in the synthesis of zeolitic material. Adsorption experiments were carried out using analytical-grade aqueous solutions of calcium (Ca2+) and magnesium (Mg2+), each prepared at an initial concentration of 1,000 mg/L. These solutions were also obtained from Sigma-Aldrich.

sec.title: Synthesis of zeolite
sec.p: The production of magnesium-enriched zeolite from talc was executed through a combination of alkaline fusion and hydrothermal conversion, following the protocol detailed in41. Initially, the raw talc was mechanically milled for 6 h using a ball mill to obtain a fine powder with particle sizes ranging from 15 μm to 100 μm. A measured quantity of 5 g of this powdered talc was then blended with 2.5 g of NaOH pellets. The mixture was thoroughly homogenized and finely ground using an agate mortar before undergoing thermal treatment. This fusion process was conducted in a muffle furnace at 550 °C for a duration of 5 h. Post-fusion, the solidified product was reground into finer particles (50–150 μm) using the agate mortar. The refined material was subsequently dispersed in 50 mL of distilled water and stirred continuously at 500 rpm for 12 h at a constant temperature of 70 °C. The resulting suspension was transferred into a Teflon-lined stainless-steel autoclave housed within a Parr reactor. Hydrothermal transformation was then carried out in a digitally controlled muffle furnace at 90 °C for 4 h. Upon completion of the reaction, the system was allowed to cool to ambient temperature. The solid products were recovered by centrifugation at 300 rpm for 15 min, washed multiple times with distilled water to remove residual alkaline impurities, and then dried at 65 °C for 10 h. The final product was designated as Mg.ZA (magnesium zeolite A) for use in subsequent material characterization and adsorption studies.

sec.title: Instrumentation for characterization
sec.p: To evaluate the crystalline phases and structural properties of both raw and synthesized materials, X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was performed using a PANalytical Empyrean diffractometer, operating over a 2θ range of 0°–70°. Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), employing a Shimadzu FTIR-8400 S spectrometer with a scanning range of 400–4000 cm⁻¹, was used to monitor changes in chemical bonding and functional groups throughout the synthesis process. The morphological features of the natural talc and the resulting zeolitic material were assessed using a scanning electron microscope (SEM), specifically the Gemini Zeiss Ultra 55. Prior to imaging, samples were coated with a thin conductive gold layer via sputter coating to enhance imaging resolution. Surface area and porosity characteristics were measured using a Beckman Coulter SA3100 surface area analyzer. Nitrogen adsorption–desorption isotherms were generated after degassing the samples under vacuum to determine specific surface area values via the BET method.

sec.title: Sampling and analysis of raw water
sec.p: An extensive water sampling campaign was carried out across the Siwa Oasis region in February 2022 to capture a representative profile of available water resources. A total of 120 water samples were collected from 110 strategically selected sites, encompassing both shallow and deep aquifers (Fig. S1). The primary aquifer systems sampled included the Nubian Sandstone Aquifer System (NSSS) and the Tertiary Carbonate Aquifer (TCA), which are the dominant sources of groundwater used for drinking, agriculture, and domestic needs in the region. Supplementary samples were obtained from alternative water bodies, including six springs, six drainage channels, and five surface lakes. To maintain the chemical integrity of the samples, they were immediately stored in iceboxes at a temperature of 4 °C and transported to the laboratory for further analysis. A comprehensive set of physico-chemical tests was conducted to assess the water quality. The results indicated that a significant number of wells exhibited concentrations of calcium and magnesium that surpassed permissible thresholds established for potable and agricultural use. These elevated hardness levels pose potential ecological threats and public health concerns, particularly with respect to long-term impacts on local aquatic environments and water usability for human consumption.

sec.title: Fixed-bed column adsorption studies
sec.p: A continuous-flow fixed-bed column system was employed to assess the efficiency of the synthesized Mg.ZA material in eliminating Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions from real groundwater samples. The experimental setup consisted of a vertical borosilicate glass column measuring 15 cm in height and 2 cm in internal diameter. The column was uniformly packed with Mg.ZA powder (50–150 μm), which was held in place using a layer of polyethylene wool at the base, reinforced by a plastic mesh to prevent adsorbent migration during operation. Groundwater was introduced into the column using a peristaltic pump that ensured a stable and controlled flow rate of 5 mL/min. Throughout the experiment, the influent pH was maintained at an unadjusted value of 7.0, and the packed-bed depth was varied between 1 cm and 3 cm to evaluate its effect on performance. Effluent samples were collected every 60 min to monitor the concentration of target ions and assess removal efficiency over time.

The column system operated under stable and uniform flow throughout all runs. The influent was delivered using a peristaltic pump at a constant flow rate (5 mL/min). For the 3 cm bed, the empty-bed contact time (EBCT) was approximately 1.9 min and the superficial velocity was about 1.59 cm/min (2.65 × 10−4 m/s), indicating a laminar flow regime. No variation in flow rate or effluent pattern was observed during the 1,740 min of operation, confirming stable hydraulic behavior without noticeable channeling, wall effects, or clogging. These conditions ensured consistent mass transfer and reproducible adsorption performance across all column tests.

This systematic approach allowed for a comprehensive evaluation of the adsorption dynamics and operational efficiency of the fixed-bed column in real-time ion removal from groundwater.

sec.title: Evaluation of calcium and magnesium hardness in Siwa groundwater
sec.p: Groundwater in Siwa Oasis contains Mg2+ = 609.54 mg/L and Ca2+ = 325.40 mg/L, yielding total hardness = 3312.61 mg/L as CaCO3 (calculated from standard Ca/Mg→CaCO3 factors)17,49, which exceeds the WHO recommended aesthetic limit (500 mg/L as CaCO3) by over sixfold and classifies the water as extremely hard (Table 1)50–52. Although Ca and Mg are essential, these levels raise concern: Mg2+ far surpasses its ~ 50 mg/L taste threshold and is associated with gastrointestinal disturbance at high intake53–55, while elevated Ca2+ (> 150 mg/L) may contribute to stone formation in susceptible individuals47,56,57. Hardness at these concentrations also threatens soil structure (Mg-driven deflocculation) and irrigation performance58,59, and may disrupt aquatic ionic balance and community composition60. These findings underscore the need for effective hardness-removal treatment, motivating the present evaluation of talc-derived, magnesium-enriched zeolite-A (Mg.ZA) as a low-cost ion-exchange adsorbent suitable for batch and fixed-bed applications in Siwa and similar arid regions.

sec.title: Characterization of the used adsorbent
sec.p: X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis confirmed the transformation of the talc precursor’s layered silicate structure into a crystalline zeolitic framework, specifically zeolite-A (LTA-type), with minor sodalite traces (Fig. 2A.I). The raw talc showed distinct peaks at 2θ = 9.48°, 19.21°, 28.62°, and 36.31°, consistent with its monoclinic phase (PDF#29-1493), while the synthesized Mg.ZA exhibited characteristic reflections of cubic zeolite-A (PDF#00-038-0241), with an average crystallite size of ~ 58 nm (Fig. 2A. II)37,41. SEM images revealed a clear morphological shift from the smooth, flaky talc layers (Fig. 2B) to cubic and equant particles typical of zeolite-A (Fig. 2C). EDX analysis confirmed the Mg-rich nature of the zeolite, with major elements including Si, O, Mg, Na, and Ca—reflecting both the talc composition and synthesis conditions using NaOH (Fig. S2). Textural properties assessed via N₂ adsorption–desorption isotherms showed a Type IV curve with H3 hysteresis (P/P₀ = 0.6–1.0), indicating a mixed micro–mesoporous structure (Fig. S3)41. Pores ranged from 1.5 to 10 nm, dominated by ~ 3 nm size, with an average diameter of 4.2 nm41. The synthesized Mg.ZA exhibited a high BET surface area of 187 m2/g, highlighting its suitability for ion adsorption in water treatment applications.

sec.title: Effect of pH
sec.p: The solution pH plays a fundamental role in governing the adsorption process, primarily by affecting both the ionic speciation of metal contaminants and the surface chemistry of the adsorbent material61. To explore this influence, the adsorption efficiency of the synthesized magnesium silicate zeolite (Mg.ZA) was systematically examined across a pH range of 2 to 8. The experimental setup was standardized with a contact time of 60 min, ambient temperature (~ 20 °C), 100 mL of solution volume, initial ion concentration fixed at 100 mg/L, and a constant Mg.ZA dosage of 0.3 g/L. These controlled conditions enabled a precise evaluation of the pH-dependent adsorption behavior for both Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions. The results revealed a significant enhancement in adsorption performance as the solution pH increased from acidic to near-neutral values. Maximum adsorption capacities were recorded at pH 7, reaching 73.4 mg/g for Ca2+ and 51.6 mg/g for Mg2+ (Fig. 3A). This improvement is closely associated with the gradual reduction in hydrogen ion (H⁺) concentration as the pH rises. Under strongly acidic conditions (pH 2–4), an abundance of H⁺ ions competes with the divalent metal ions for active binding sites on the zeolitic surface. This competition weakens metal uptake due to the preferential occupation of adsorption or ion exchange sites by protons41. As the pH increases toward neutral levels, the suppressive effect of hydrogen ions diminishes, allowing more effective interaction between Ca2+/Mg2+ ions and the negatively charged adsorption sites.

Moreover, the enhancement of adsorption at near-neutral pH can also be attributed to the deprotonation of surface hydroxyl groups on the Mg.ZA surface, which leads to an increasingly negative surface charge. This electrostatic environment facilitates stronger attraction and binding of positively charged metal ions, significantly improving ion exchange efficiency. The observed adsorption peak at pH 7, therefore, represents an optimal balance between minimized proton competition and maximized surface reactivity. Beyond pH 7, however, a sharp decline in adsorption capacities was observed for both Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions. This decrease is largely due to two interrelated factors. First, in alkaline conditions, the formation of metal hydroxide species (e.g., Ca(OH)₂, Mg(OH)₂) reduces the concentration of free divalent ions in solution, thereby limiting their availability for adsorption62. Second, elevated pH levels may partially compromise the structural integrity of zeolite materials, potentially leading to dissolution or destabilization of surface-active sites, further diminishing adsorption performance63. This decline underscores the sensitivity of zeolitic materials to high-pH environments, necessitating careful control of solution chemistry during practical applications.

Based on the measured pH values and the estimated pH at the zero point of charge (pHPZC), the surface-charge transition for the synthesized Mg.ZA adsorbent was found to occur around pH 5.4 for Ca2+ and pH 5.8 for Mg2+. These values are consistent with those reported for magnesium-silicate and zeolite-A–type materials in similar adsorption systems. Accordingly, at pH values above these points, the Mg.ZA surface becomes negatively charged, favoring electrostatic attraction and ion-exchange with the divalent cations. This explains the enhanced uptake observed near neutral conditions (pH ≈ 7), where the negative surface potential promotes interaction with Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions. Conversely, at pH < pHPZC, protonation of surface sites and competition from H⁺ ions reduce adsorption efficiency. The close correspondence between these pHPZC values and the experimental adsorption trends confirms that the observed behavior reflects the intrinsic surface-charge characteristics of the Mg.ZA framework and the nature of the studied hardness ions.

From an environmental engineering perspective, the efficient performance of Mg.ZA within the pH range of 6 to 7 is highly promising. This range coincides with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s recommended pH window for the discharge and treatment of industrial and municipal wastewater streams64. As such, Mg.ZA demonstrates considerable potential for real-world implementation in water treatment facilities, where natural or slightly adjusted pH conditions are common.

sec.title: Effect of contact time
sec.p: To elucidate the time-dependent adsorption behavior of the synthesized magnesium silicate zeolite (Mg.ZA), a comprehensive kinetic study was carried out over a contact period ranging from 5 to 840 min. All experimental conditions were carefully controlled, maintaining a constant initial metal ion concentration of 100 mg/L, solution volume of 100 mL, ambient temperature at 293 K, and a pH of 7 for both Ca2+ and Mg2+ systems. An adsorbent dose of 0.3 g/L was employed to ensure uniformity across trials. This design aimed to investigate the impact of contact duration on the adsorption kinetics and capacity of Mg.ZA for divalent hardness ions.

The adsorption profiles revealed a distinct two-phase pattern (Fig. 3B). During the initial stage of the experiment, there was a rapid increase in the removal of Ca2+ and Mg2+, attributed to the high availability of accessible and energetically favorable adsorption sites on the Mg.ZA surface. These sites readily interacted with free metal ions, facilitating efficient binding and resulting in significant ion uptake within the first 240 min65. As contact time extended, the adsorption rate began to decelerate gradually, eventually reaching a plateau near 400 min, where no further appreciable increase in ion sequestration was observed. This stabilization point marked the onset of equilibrium conditions, wherein the rate of adsorption equaled the rate of desorption, and the system’s adsorption capacity was effectively saturated. At equilibrium, the maximum adsorption capacities recorded were 104.2 mg/g for Ca2+ and 80.1 mg/g for Mg2+, indicating a stronger affinity of Mg.ZA toward calcium ions (Fig. 3B). This selectivity may be attributed to the smaller hydration radius and higher binding energy of Ca2+ compared to Mg2+, which facilitates more favorable interactions with the zeolitic surface. The decline in adsorption rate over time can be explained by the progressive occupation of the active functional groups on the Mg.ZA particles. As more adsorption sites became occupied, fewer remained available for additional metal ions, resulting in a lower probability of ion binding. Furthermore, the diffusion of ions into less accessible interior pores likely became rate-limiting during the latter stages, contributing to the observed kinetic plateau66. This equilibrium phase reflects not only the efficiency but also the stability and predictability of Mg.ZA as an adsorbent material under fixed operational conditions. The transition from rapid initial uptake to steady-state equilibrium underscores the material’s suitability for practical water treatment applications, particularly in continuous flow or batch systems with defined residence times. The data obtained confirm the capability of Mg.ZA to act as an effective and reliable medium for the removal of water hardness-causing ions. The fast initial adsorption indicates a strong potential for short-contact-time applications, while the high equilibrium capacity ensures that the material remains effective over extended treatment durations. These insights are critical for optimizing contact time in practical scenarios and further validate the use of Mg.ZA as a promising candidate for sustainable ion removal technologies.

sec.title: Starting concentration
sec.p: The effect of initial ion concentration on adsorption efficiency was examined for Ca2+ and Mg2+ using the synthesized magnesium-silicate zeolite (Mg.ZA) over 50–450 mg/L. All other conditions were fixed (contact time 24 h, adsorbent dose 0.3 g/L, solution volume 100 mL, pH 7, 293 K) so that only the starting concentration varied. The experimental results demonstrated a clear and consistent increase in adsorption capacity as the initial concentrations of Ca2+ and Mg2+ increased (Fig. 3C). This trend can be attributed to the enhanced concentration gradient between the solution and the adsorbent surface, which serves as a driving force for mass transfer. Higher ion concentrations improve the frequency of collision between metal ions and active binding sites, facilitating a more efficient diffusion process and leading to greater adsorption at the surface of Mg.ZA67. At lower concentrations, many adsorption sites remain unoccupied due to limited interaction opportunities with the ions. However, as the concentration of Ca2+ and Mg2+ rises, a greater proportion of these sites are accessed, increasing the rate and extent of ion capture. This behavior is consistent with classical adsorption theory, which suggests that higher solute concentrations enhance transport phenomena and adsorption kinetics during the initial stages of contact68.

With increasing concentration, the adsorption capacity eventually reached a plateau as the active sites on the Mg.ZA surface became saturated. Once these sites were fully occupied, no further uptake occurred regardless of ion concentration67,68. At equilibrium, the maximum adsorption capacities were 248.6 mg/g for Ca2+ and 198.7 mg/g for Mg2+ (Fig. 3C), indicating the material’s strong affinity for divalent hardness ions. The higher Ca2+ uptake compared to Mg2+ is attributed to differences in their hydration radii and energies, where the smaller, less hydrated Ca2+ interacts more strongly with the negatively charged zeolitic surface69,70. These findings have significant environmental and industrial implications. The ability of Mg.ZA to maintain high adsorption efficiency at elevated contaminant levels demonstrates its strong potential for treating heavily mineralized groundwater and industrial effluents rich in hardness ions. The well-defined equilibrium profiles and saturation behavior also enable accurate prediction of performance in practical systems, supporting the design and optimization of treatment processes. Moreover, the effective removal of Ca2+ and Mg2+ indicates potential for selective separation and recovery of these ions, offering additional opportunities in resource recycling and reuse. Overall, the exceptional uptake capacities and concentration-dependent adsorption behavior confirm the viability of Mg.ZA as a robust, high-performance adsorbent for sustainable water treatment applications.

sec.title: Solid dosage
sec.p: A series of adsorption experiments were conducted to evaluate how varying the amount of Mg.ZA adsorbent influences the removal efficiency of calcium (Ca2+) and magnesium (Mg2+) ions. The dosage of Mg.ZA was systematically altered between 0.1 g/L and 0.8 g/L, while maintaining consistent experimental parameters: a solution volume of 100 mL, contact time of 24 h, initial ion concentration of 100 mg/L, pH adjusted to 7, and a fixed temperature of 293 K. This design ensured that any observed variation in adsorption performance could be directly attributed to changes in adsorbent mass, eliminating potential interference from other operational factors.

The results, illustrated in Fig. 3D, show a clear positive correlation between adsorbent dosage and ion removal efficiency across the tested range. As the Mg.ZA dosage increased, so did the adsorption performance for both target ions. This enhancement can be attributed to the greater availability of active surface sites and increased total surface area provided by the higher adsorbent quantity. A larger mass of Mg.ZA introduces more binding domains—such as silanol and alumina groups—on the particle surface, thereby increasing the probability of ion–site interaction and improving the overall ion capture rate71. The observed adsorption behavior aligns with the surface saturation theory, which suggests that an increase in adsorbent mass raises the likelihood of ion adsorption until a saturation point is approached. Specifically, for Ca2+, removal efficiency improved progressively with dosage: from 10.4% at 0.1 g/L to 26.8% (0.2 g/L), 40.2% (0.3 g/L), 57.8% (0.4 g/L), 74.4% (0.5 g/L) and peaking at 87.2% at 0.8 g/L. A similar trend was recorded for Mg2+, with removal rates increasing from 8.2% at 0.1 g/L to 70.2% at 0.8 g/L (Fig. 3D). These results clearly demonstrate that the availability of more active sites facilitates enhanced uptake of metal ions, particularly when working within low to moderate concentration ranges.

From a practical perspective, this saturation behavior has important implications. Although increasing adsorbent dosage can enhance performance, excessive amounts may lead to material wastage and higher operational costs without substantial gains in efficiency. Therefore, identifying the optimal dosage—such as 0.7–0.8 g/L in this case—is crucial for designing cost-effective and scalable water treatment systems. The strong adsorption performance observed at relatively low dosages also positions Mg.ZA as an economically viable and sustainable material for treating water hardness, particularly in regions facing resource limitations. Moreover, these findings underscore Mg.ZA’s potential not only in water softening applications but also in broader environmental remediation strategies. Its high removal efficiency, even at modest dosages, makes it a promising candidate for wastewater treatment facilities targeting divalent metal ions. Furthermore, the material’s capacity to sequester Ca2+ and Mg2+ suggests its applicability in selective recovery processes, where these ions can be extracted and reused in various industrial sectors, including agriculture, pharmaceuticals, and mineral processing.

sec.title: Intra-particle diffusion behavior
sec.p: To further elucidate the adsorption mechanism of Mg.ZA and provide a deeper understanding of the internal transport phenomena, intra-particle diffusion analysis was conducted. This approach aimed to dissect the multi-phase adsorption behavior of Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions and to identify the underlying kinetic pathways governing their interaction with the synthesized adsorbent. The adsorption profiles, as depicted in Fig. 4, display distinct non-linear, multi-slope characteristics, revealing three consecutive adsorption stages. These stages indicate that the adsorption process involves a combination of surface interaction, internal diffusion, and equilibrium saturation mechanisms operating simultaneously and sequentially72.

list-item.label: A.
list-item.p: The initial adsorption phase is characterized by the rapid uptake of metal ions at the outer surface of Mg.ZA particles. This stage is dominated by physical and ion-exchange interactions, where Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions bind directly to easily accessible surface-active sites. The high availability of vacant adsorption domains facilitates this fast removal, making it particularly effective in the early period of the process. This rapid interaction is indicative of a strong affinity between the divalent cations and the surface functional groups, and it plays a vital role in determining the overall kinetics and initial efficiency of the system (Fig. 4).

list-item.label: B.
list-item.p: Stage II – internal diffusion and pore interaction.

Following surface site saturation, the system transitions into a slower phase driven primarily by intra-particle diffusion. In this intermediate stage, metal ions begin to diffuse into the internal porous matrix of Mg.ZA, where additional binding sites are located (Fig. 4). This migration occurs through both mesoporous and microporous channels, enabling continued ion removal beyond the capacity of the external surface alone. The rate-limiting step here is the diffusion of ions through the porous network and their subsequent interaction with internal functional groups via mechanisms such as complexation or deeper ion exchange73,74. The structure of Mg.ZA—characterized by high surface area and hierarchical porosity—facilitates this sustained uptake.

list-item.label: C.
list-item.p: Stage III – equilibrium and adsorbent saturation.

The final stage is defined by the stabilization of adsorption capacity, marking the point at which all available adsorption sites—both surface-bound and internal—have been occupied (Fig. 4). At this equilibrium phase, further removal of Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions becomes negligible. Ion retention is maintained through weaker interactions such as van der Waals forces, electrostatic stabilization, or pore entrapment75,76. This plateau indicates that the system has reached its thermodynamic limit under the prevailing experimental conditions, and no additional ions can be immobilized without regeneration or structural modification of the adsorbent.

sec.p: The identification of this three-phase adsorption progression provides a comprehensive kinetic framework for understanding the behavior of Mg.ZA in aqueous environments. Initially, the efficiency is strongly influenced by the abundance of accessible surface sites, which ensures rapid contaminant removal. As these are progressively occupied, the reliance on intra-particle diffusion underscores the importance of pore connectivity, particle size, and structural openness in sustaining adsorption performance. The saturation phase, although indicative of capacity limits, reflects the robustness of Mg.ZA under long-term or high-load conditions. From an application standpoint, this insight is invaluable for optimizing the design of treatment systems using Mg.ZA. It informs decisions on contact time, particle size distribution, and flow dynamics in both batch and continuous operations. Moreover, the ability of Mg.ZA to sustain adsorption through multiple diffusion and interaction stages highlights its viability for scalable water treatment technologies targeting divalent ions. In summary, the intra-particle diffusion study confirms that the adsorption of Ca2+ and Mg2+ onto Mg.ZA follows a complex but predictable multi-stage mechanism. The integration of surface-level binding, pore diffusion, and equilibrium saturation illustrates the adsorbent’s capacity for high-efficiency ion removal, reinforcing its potential role in environmentally sustainable remediation strategies.

sec.title: Kinetic modeling
sec.p: A comprehensive understanding of adsorption kinetics is essential for elucidating the underlying mechanisms that control contaminant uptake in adsorbent systems. Specifically, adsorption kinetics shed light on the interplay between surface interaction dynamics and mass transfer processes, both of which critically influence the rate and efficiency of pollutant removal over time77,78. In this study, the adsorption behavior of calcium (Ca2+) and magnesium (Mg2+) ions onto the synthesized Mg.ZA adsorbent was investigated using two widely applied kinetic models: the pseudo-first-order (PFO) and pseudo-second-order (PSO) models. These models offer complementary perspectives, enabling a more complete interpretation of the physical and chemical mechanisms involved in ion adsorption. The PFO kinetic model emphasizes the role of physisorption, where the rate of adsorption is directly related to the number of unoccupied active sites on the adsorbent surface. It is particularly suitable for systems dominated by weak, non-covalent interactions such as van der Waals forces and electrostatic attractions. In contrast, the PSO model is grounded in chemisorption theory and assumes that the adsorption rate is influenced by the formation of stronger chemical bonds, such as covalent surface complexation. The comparative application of both models allows for a nuanced analysis of the adsorption mechanism and the relative contribution of each interaction type78.

To evaluate model suitability, nonlinear regression analysis was employed to fit the experimental kinetic data for Ca2+ and Mg2+ adsorption. The quality of fit was assessed based on correlation coefficients (R2) and chi-squared error values (χ2), providing a statistical basis for model comparison. As shown in Table 2; Fig. 5A and B, the PFO model demonstrated a stronger correlation with the experimental data than the PSO model. The regression curves presented in Fig. 5A illustrate a near-exact match between the PFO-predicted and observed adsorption capacities, while the PSO model (Fig. 5B) exhibited moderate deviations. The theoretical equilibrium adsorption capacities estimated by the PFO model—105.3 mg/g for Ca2+ and 80.3 mg/g for Mg2+—aligned closely with the experimentally measured values, reinforcing the conclusion that physical interactions are the dominant forces driving ion uptake onto Mg.ZA76,77. The superior predictive power of the PFO model suggests that the adsorption process is primarily governed by physical mechanisms, such as ion-dipole attractions and van der Waals forces, rather than covalent or chemical bonding. However, the reasonable fit of the PSO model also points to the presence of secondary chemical interactions. These may include hydrogen bonding and the partial formation of metal–surface complexes, which, although less dominant, contribute to overall adsorption by enhancing ion retention at specific sites76.

Importantly, the dual contribution of physical and chemical interactions supports the hypothesis of a sequential or layered adsorption mechanism. Initially, divalent ions may form strong interactions with surface-active sites, establishing a primary adsorption layer. Subsequently, weaker physical forces can facilitate the formation of additional ion layers on top of the initial monolayer, increasing the total adsorption capacity. This multilayer adsorption phenomenon has been observed in other porous materials and may explain the high ion uptake observed for Mg.ZA78. In summary, kinetic modeling reveals that the adsorption of Ca2+ and Mg2+ onto Mg.ZA is predominantly controlled by physical adsorption processes, as evidenced by the superior fit of the PFO model. Nonetheless, the presence of chemisorptive contributions indicates that the system exhibits a complex interaction landscape, involving both reversible physisorption and site-specific chemical bonding.

sec.title: Classic isotherm models
sec.p: Equilibrium investigations are critical to characterizing the interaction between adsorbent materials and dissolved contaminants, providing essential insights into the capacity, affinity, and mechanism of ion binding under steady-state conditions. These studies are central to understanding how pollutants partition between the aqueous phase and the adsorbent surface once the adsorption process has reached dynamic equilibrium. More importantly, equilibrium modeling enables a quantitative evaluation of system behavior, assisting in the optimization and scale-up of adsorption technologies. The application of isotherm models helps decode three core aspects of the system: (i) the affinity of the adsorbent for target ions at the solid–liquid interface, (ii) the theoretical maximum ion loading capacity, and (iii) the heterogeneity or uniformity of adsorption site energies across the material’s surface76,79. In this study, the equilibrium profiles of Ca2+ and Mg2+ adsorption onto Mg.ZA were assessed using three well-established isotherm models: Langmuir (Fig. 5C), Freundlich (Fig. 5D), and Dubinin–Radushkevich (D–R) (Fig. 5E). Experimental data were fitted through nonlinear regression techniques, and the quality of each model’s representation was determined based on the correlation coefficient (R2) and the chi-squared error (χ2), as summarized in Table 2.

Among the models evaluated, the Langmuir isotherm provided the best fit to the experimental data, as evidenced by the highest R2 values and the lowest χ2 residuals (Table 2). This strong agreement indicates that adsorption likely occurs on a structurally uniform surface, where all available binding sites exhibit equal affinity toward the metal ions77,79. According to the Langmuir theory, adsorption proceeds via monolayer coverage, with each binding site accommodating a single ion without interactions between adsorbed species. The dimensionless Langmuir separation factor (RL), calculated for both Ca2+ and Mg2+, was found to be less than 1, confirming that the adsorption process is thermodynamically favorable across the tested concentration range80. The model also estimated the maximum monolayer adsorption capacities (Qmax) to be 268.8 mg/g for Ca2+ and 206.9 mg/g for Mg2+, highlighting the remarkable uptake performance of Mg.ZA for both divalent ions under optimized conditions.

While the Langmuir model provided structural insights, the Dubinin–Radushkevich (D–R) isotherm offered valuable information regarding the energetic nature of the adsorption process. Unlike empirical isotherms, the D–R model incorporates the concept of mean adsorption energy (E), which serves as a diagnostic indicator of the dominant interaction mechanism. The magnitude of E can be interpreted to differentiate among physical adsorption (E < 8 kJ/mol), mixed-mode adsorption (8 ≤ E ≤ 16 kJ/mol), and purely chemical adsorption involving covalent bonding (E > 16 kJ/mol)81,82. The calculated adsorption energy (E = 8–16 kJ/mol) suggests a mixed physisorption–chemisorption mechanism, where both weak electrostatic attraction and stronger surface-specific interactions occur. These energies align with the interaction of hydrated Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions with the negatively charged surface sites of Mg.ZA, dominated by Si–O–Mg, Si–O–Al, and –OH groups. The hydroxyl-bearing groups contribute to hydrogen bonding and partial surface complexation, complementing the electrostatic and ion-exchange interactions implied by the silicate–oxygen framework. Together, these surface features explain the moderate adsorption energy values observed. The proposed dual-mechanism behavior implies that the initial stages of ion removal are primarily governed by weak physical forces, such as van der Waals interactions and electrostatic attractions. These interactions allow rapid binding and partial reversibility. As the process progresses, more specific chemical interactions—including hydrogen bonding and surface complexation—occur, leading to stronger and more stable attachment of ions to the internal and external active sites of Mg.ZA. This layered interaction not only enhances adsorption efficiency but also offers functional flexibility, particularly relevant for systems where both strong binding and ease of regeneration are important.

These findings collectively underscore the versatility of Mg.ZA as a hybrid adsorbent, capable of efficient removal of water hardness ions through a combination of monolayer adsorption and energy-diverse interactions. The superior fit of the Langmuir model confirms a homogeneous distribution of active sites and supports the notion that monolayer adsorption predominates under the conditions tested. Meanwhile, the insights from the D–R model reveal that both physical and chemical mechanisms contribute to the overall process, enhancing the robustness and adaptability of Mg.ZA across varying contaminant concentrations. In summary, the equilibrium study demonstrates that Mg.ZA exhibits high selectivity and capacity for Ca2+ and Mg2+ removal, facilitated by a surface architecture that supports monolayer binding and energetic heterogeneity. This dual mechanism, combining the structural predictability of Langmuir behavior with the energetic complexity indicated by the D–R model, makes Mg.ZA an exceptionally promising material for advanced water purification and ion separation applications.

sec.title: Advanced isotherm models
sec.p: To gain deeper insight into the molecular-level interactions governing the adsorption of Ca2+ and Mg2+ onto the synthesized Mg.ZA adsorbent, a statistical physics modeling approach was employed. This advanced framework extends beyond classical isotherm models by integrating both steric and energetic factors to capture the adsorption behavior under equilibrium conditions with greater precision. The model elucidates how metal ions interact with discrete, energetically independent receptor sites on the adsorbent surface and allows for the characterization of site occupation, spatial orientation, and binding energy. The parameters derived from the advanced (statistical-physics) isotherm model provide quantitative insight into the adsorption geometry and the physicochemical nature of the Mg.ZA surface. The parameter n (ions per active site) describes the number of adsorbed ions accommodated at a single binding site. Values of n > 1 indicate multi-ionic or vertical stacking at adsorption sites, reflecting enhanced ion–ion interaction on the zeolitic surface. This parameter thus characterizes the spatial configuration and cooperative behavior of ions during surface loading.

sec.p: The parameter Nm (adsorption-site density) corresponds to the total number of available active sites per gram of adsorbent, representing the surface heterogeneity, ion-exchange capacity, and density of reactive centers such as Si–O–Mg, Si–O–Al, and –OH groups. Higher Nm values imply a greater number of energetically favorable sites contributing to the overall capacity. Collectively, these parameters reveal the structural and energetic diversity of adsorption sites and bridge the gap between molecular-level adsorption behavior and the macroscopic uptake performance observed for Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions on Mg.ZA.

The fundamental parameters (the density of adsorption sites (Nm, mg/g), the number of ions adsorbed per active site (n), the adsorption energy (ΔE, kJ/mol), and the theoretical saturation adsorption capacity (Qsat, mg/g)) were extracted through multivariable nonlinear regression fitting with Monolayer model of single energetic site using the Levenberg–Marquardt optimization algorithm. The model assumes that adsorption occurs via a monolayer configuration with no lateral interactions among adsorbed species, aligning with the principles of single-site adsorption mechanisms (Fig. 5F; Table 2).

In this study, Ca2+ and Mg2+ exhibited n-values of 2.12 and 2.81, respectively, demonstrating that individual active sites on Mg.ZA are capable of accommodating multiple ions in a vertically oriented configuration. This result suggests the presence of multi-ionic interaction mechanisms that enhance adsorption capacity through spatial stacking and ion clustering83,84. The variation in ion loading per site can be attributed to differences in ionic properties such as hydration radius, charge density, and electrostatic mobility. On average, each binding site could retain up to three Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions. The total number of occupied sites (Nm) was estimated to be 126.9 mg/g for Ca2+ and 73.6 mg/g for Mg2+. These values, when combined with the respective n-values, yielded theoretical saturation capacities (Qsat) of 269.0 mg/g for Ca2+ and 206.8 mg/g for Mg2+, closely aligning with the experimental maximum adsorption capacities obtained in equilibrium studies. These findings emphasize the strong correlation between structural design and adsorption performance, and they validate the model’s ability to predict real-world adsorption behavior.

The calculated ΔE values for Ca2+ and Mg2+ were below 8 kJ mol⁻¹, confirming that the adsorption process is primarily physisorption-dominated. These energies fall within the range associated with weak electrostatic interactions (2–50 kJ/mol), hydrogen bonding (< 30 kJ/mol), and dipole–dipole forces (2–29 kJ/mol) between the hydrated ions and the negatively charged surface of Mg.ZA67,85. The presence of Si–O–Mg, Si–O–Al, and surface –OH groups enhances these interactions by providing multiple adsorption domains that stabilize the hydrated cations through hydrogen bonding and localized polarization effects (Fig. 6). Mechanistically, the low ΔE values indicate that ion uptake proceeds through a multi-stage physical adsorption pathway. In the initial stage, hydrated Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions are rapidly attracted to the zeolitic framework via outer-sphere electrostatic forces, forming a loosely bound primary layer. As surface coverage increases, secondary interactions—mainly hydrogen bonding with –OH groups and weak surface complexation at silicate edges—develop, reinforcing the stability of adsorbed ions without transitioning to chemisorption. The statistical-physics parameter n > 1 further supports this interpretation, signifying multi-ionic vertical stacking at each active site, which promotes multilayer adsorption while preserving reversibility.

The obtained ΔE values were negative, confirming that the process is exothermic and spontaneous under the studied conditions. The combination of moderate binding energies, multilayer stacking, and accessible surface functionality explains the high adsorption capacity and the facile desorption behavior of Mg.ZA. Consequently, the material demonstrates efficient, reversible, and energetically favorable ion uptake, making it highly suitable for cyclic water-softening applications and large-scale groundwater remediation systems.

sec.title: Regeneration and recyclability of Mg.ZA
sec.p: The regeneration and recyclability of the synthesized magnesium silicate zeolite (Mg.ZA) were investigated under batch conditions to assess its stability and potential for repeated use. Five successive adsorption–desorption cycles were carried out using 100 mL of 100 mg/L Ca2+ or Mg2+ solutions at pH 7 and 293 K. In each cycle, 0.3 g/L of Mg.ZA was contacted with the solution and agitated for 24 h to reach equilibrium. After each adsorption step, the exhausted adsorbent was regenerated using 0.1 M NaCl solution to desorb the retained ions through ion exchange, followed by washing with deionized water to neutral pH and drying at 80 °C for six hours before reuse in the next cycle.

The results confirmed that Mg.ZA maintained high removal efficiency across all cycles, demonstrating strong structural stability and reusability. In the first cycle, the adsorption capacities were measured as 104.2 mg/g for Ca2+ and 80.1 mg/g for Mg2+. After five consecutive regeneration cycles, the capacities slightly decreased to 91.3 mg/g for Ca2+ and 69.4 mg/g for Mg2+, corresponding to overall retention rates of approximately 88% and 86%, respectively. The small decline in adsorption capacity can be attributed to partial site occupation by residual ions and minor pore constriction resulting from repeated ion-exchange operations.

The consistent retention of adsorption performance indicates that the ion-exchange and physisorption processes in Mg.ZA are highly reversible and energetically favorable, in line with the low adsorption energy (ΔE < 8 kJ/mol) derived from the statistical-physics model. The slightly higher regeneration stability observed for Ca2+ compared with Mg2+ reflects the stronger electrostatic affinity of calcium ions, which possess a smaller hydration radius and higher field strength. Overall, the high recyclability and stable performance of Mg.ZA confirm its potential as a cost-effective and sustainable adsorbent for water hardness removal. Its ability to maintain more than 85% of its initial capacity after five regeneration cycles using a simple NaCl regenerant demonstrates both its practical efficiency and long-term applicability for repeated use in groundwater treatment and industrial water-softening systems.

sec.title: The experimental performance of the Mg.ZA bed
sec.p: The effect of bed thickness in fixed-bed column configurations was critically evaluated to determine its influence on the removal efficiency of Ca2+ and Mg2+ using Mg.ZA as the adsorbent. Bed depths of 1 cm (2.7 g), 2 cm (5.4 g), and 3 cm (8.1 g) were systematically tested to assess their role in modifying adsorption behavior and overall column performance under continuous flow conditions (Fig. 7). The experiments were conducted under standardized operational parameters, including an initial ion concentration of 25 mg/L, a solution pH of 7, a constant flow rate of 5 mL/min, and a total operational runtime of 1740 min. This controlled design enabled direct comparison of adsorption dynamics as a function of bed height.

The results clearly demonstrated that increasing the Mg.ZA bed thickness substantially enhanced both the longevity of column operation and the adsorption efficiency for divalent ions (Fig. 7A, B; Table 3). For calcium ion removal, a pronounced shift in breakthrough times was observed as bed thickness increased. Specifically, breakthrough occurred at approximately 600 min for the 1 cm bed, extended to 660 min for the 2 cm bed, and further to 900 min for the 3 cm configuration (Fig. 6A). Notably, the 3 cm bed did not reach exhaustion even after 1740 min, suggesting superior retention capacity under extended flow conditions. The total volume of treated water (~ 9 L) further confirmed the influence of bed height on decontamination performance. For the 3 cm bed, the column received 1567.5 mg of Ca2+ in total (Mtotal), out of which 1006.6 mg were effectively captured (Qtotal), corresponding to a removal efficiency of approximately 82.0%. The resulting bed adsorption capacity (Cad) was calculated to be 369.0 mg, with an equilibrium adsorption capacity (Qeq) of 279.6 mg/g for Ca2+ under the given conditions (Table 3). A parallel trend was observed for magnesium ion adsorption (Fig. 7B). The 3 cm bed achieved a breakthrough at around 780 min, with no indication of column exhaustion within the test period. The total amount of Mg2+ introduced (Mtotal) was also 1567.5 mg, of which 820.0 mg were adsorbed, resulting in a removal efficiency of 75.1%. The bed adsorption capacity was determined to be 338.1 mg, and the Qeq reached 227.8 mg/g (Table 3).

The improved performance at increased bed thickness arises from coupled hydrodynamic and mass-transfer effects. A taller bed increases the empty-bed contact time (EBCT), extending the residence of the solute front within the column so that hydrated Ca2+/Mg2+ ions interact longer with surface-active sites on Mg.ZA86,87. Concomitantly, greater bed height lowers the relative influence of axial dispersion by promoting a more plug-flow-like profile; the dispersion number decreases as the ratio of bed length to particle size grows, delaying premature breakthrough and sharpening the advancing mass-transfer zone (MTZ). As the MTZ occupies a smaller fraction of the overall bed, a larger portion of the column contributes to effective uptake before the front reaches the outlet, which manifests as longer breakthrough and service times.

A thicker bed also facilitates completion of the two principal resistances that limit uptake at short contact times: film diffusion across the external boundary layer and intraparticle diffusion within the Mg.ZA pore network. With increased EBCT, ions have sufficient time to traverse the liquid film, enter the pores, and sample the internal site population, improving utilization of the adsorption-site density (Nm) inferred from the isotherm analysis. From an engineering standpoint, bed thickness is therefore a primary design lever governing breakthrough behavior, operational longevity, and total removal capacity. Under the conditions studied here, a 3 cm Mg.ZA bed provided an effective compromise—high hardness removal with extended service time—by simultaneously reducing axial dispersion, lengthening EBCT, and allowing deeper intraparticle penetration without sacrificing hydraulic stability. This relationship offers a practical sizing criterion for compact, continuous systems: increasing bed height within acceptable head-loss limits enhances decontamination efficiency, particularly at low influent concentrations and during extended operation cycles. These insights support reliable scale-up using standard fixed-bed design tools (e.g., EBCT targets and BDST-type correlations) while maintaining the mechanistic basis for performance.

sec.title: Dynamic modelling of the column
sec.p: To interpret and predict the adsorption behavior of Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions in the continuous fixed-bed column system packed with Mg.ZA, three widely recognized kinetic models—Thomas, Adams–Bohart, and Yoon–Nelson—were applied. These models are essential for evaluating the efficiency and dynamics of fixed-bed systems, particularly in simulating breakthrough curves, estimating kinetic parameters, and optimizing process performance. The dynamic modeling was executed using linear regression techniques, employing the mathematical formulations of the three models as follows:

These models facilitated a robust analysis of adsorption mechanisms and allowed for a detailed comparison between theoretical predictions and experimental observations, guiding performance optimization for real-world applications86,88.

Based on the fitting results, Thomas, Adams–Bohart, and Yoon–Nelson models yielded high and comparable fits to the Ca2+/Mg2+ column data (see R2 in Table 3), indicating consistent description of the dynamic behavior. The Thomas model provided the best overall correlation and capacity prediction under its assumptions of Langmuir-type equilibrium and plug flow with negligible axial dispersion—assumptions that align with our system’s laminar regime, uniform packing, stable flow, and short bed, where channeling or pressure-drop effects were not observed89,90. This assumption aligns with the experimental setup, as the laminar flow regime (Re < 1), uniform packing, and small particle size (50–150 μm) minimized axial dispersion and diffusion effects, validating the plug-flow and Langmuir-equilibrium conditions of the Thomas model, as also supported by the high correlation between predicted and experimental data (R2 ≈ 0.91–0.97, Table 2).

The Adams–Bohart model captured the initial breakthrough region governed predominantly by film transfer and surface reaction kinetics, while the Yoon–Nelson model offered practical service-time (τ) estimates that are geometry-agnostic and useful for design scaling86,91. Accordingly, the three models are complementary rather than conflicting: Adams–Bohart resolves early-zone transport, Thomas integrates equilibrium-driven capacity/kinetics over the full curve, and Yoon–Nelson provides concise time-to-breakthrough/saturation predictions. Together, they furnish a coherent, multi-perspective interpretation of the same fixed-bed system without conceptual contradictions, and their concurrent use strengthens confidence in the extracted dynamic parameters.

sec.title: Thomas model
sec.p: Thomas model is particularly useful for estimating maximum adsorption capacity and rate constants under varying operational conditions. The calculated determination coefficients (R2) from model fitting across different bed thicknesses indicate a strong correlation between the experimental data and the theoretical Thomas curves (Fig. 7C and D; Table 3). Interestingly, although the model showed good predictive accuracy, a subtle decline in equilibrium capacity was noted as bed thickness increased from 1 to 3 cm. This may reflect saturation effects or slight reductions in effective mass transfer per unit mass of adsorbent as flow dynamics evolve in thicker beds. Overall, the model provided reliable capacity estimates and insight into the kinetics governing the system’s performance.

sec.title: Adams-Bohart model
sec.p: The Adams–Bohart model is particularly effective in characterizing the initial region of the breakthrough curve, focusing on the early-stage mass transfer of solutes through the bed. It assumes a constant adsorption capacity and linear adsorption kinetics with respect to concentration91. The model is especially suited for evaluating saturation concentrations (N₀) and the rate constant (KAB) during the initial adsorption phase. Experimental data closely matched the Adams–Bohart predictions for different bed depths and flow conditions, as evidenced by the strong agreement in breakthrough profiles (Fig. 7E and F; Table 3). As the bed thickness increased, a consistent decline in the calculated N₀ values was observed, indicating that a thicker bed facilitates more complete usage of the adsorbent’s capacity. This inverse relationship suggests improved contaminant distribution and minimized early breakthrough due to extended residence times. The model effectively captured the transition from partial to complete utilization of the bed, making it a useful tool for system scale-up and early-stage process design.

sec.title: Yoon-Nelson model
sec.p: The Yoon–Nelson model offers a simplified yet effective approach to predicting the time required for 50% breakthrough (τ) without requiring detailed information about the adsorbent or solute. This model is particularly practical for operational planning, providing direct estimates of column lifespan under given conditions86. Model fitting results showed excellent agreement with the experimental breakthrough curves for both Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions across all bed thicknesses (Fig. 7G and H; Table 3), as demonstrated by high R2 values. For a 3 cm bed thickness, the model predicted that 50% saturation was achieved after 1309.6 min for Ca2+ and 1154.1 min for Mg2+, highlighting the extended operational lifespan of the column at increased bed depths. This confirms that higher bed thickness not only improves adsorption efficiency but also prolongs the effective usage period before regeneration is required.

The application of these dynamic models confirms that the Mg.ZA-packed fixed-bed system follows predictable and quantifiable adsorption behavior. Each model provided complementary insights: the Thomas model revealed total capacity trends; the Adams–Bohart model captured early-stage mass transfer efficiency; and the Yoon–Nelson model forecasted column service duration. Together, they establish a robust framework for designing, scaling, and optimizing Mg.ZA-based continuous flow systems for water purification. Notably, the results emphasize the critical influence of bed thickness on performance, with thicker beds demonstrating longer breakthrough times, higher removal efficiency, and greater total ion capture.

sec.title: Realistic remediation of groundwater in Siwa Oasis
sec.p: In this study, the purification of Siwa groundwater was performed using a successive column configuration designed to simulate a practical multi-stage treatment process. The approach involved four consecutive adsorption runs, where the effluent from each column stage served as the influent for the next, effectively representing four purification cycles in series. This setup aimed to mimic the behavior of continuous or modular adsorption units used in real field operations. Each cycle was operated under identical conditions (bed depth = 3 cm, flow rate = 5 mL/min, pH ≈ 7, a prolonged treatment duration of 1740 min) to ensure that variations in performance were solely due to cumulative ion reduction rather than operating parameters. This configuration allowed assessment of the progressive improvement in water quality, as successive stages further reduced residual hardness levels.

It is important to note that these successive cycles represent a staged purification process rather than regeneration–reuse testing. The method provides a realistic evaluation of Mg.ZA’s operational stability, flow performance, and hardness removal efficiency under extended continuous use, demonstrating its suitability for practical groundwater treatment applications. The groundwater utilized in the experiment was collected from multiple wells across Siwa, and its chemical composition—specifically the concentrations of calcium (Ca2+ at 609.54 mg/L) and magnesium (Mg2+ at 325.40 mg/L)—highlighted the characteristic high hardness of groundwater in desert and semi-desert aquifers. To model a more controlled and practical softening scenario, the raw water samples were diluted with distilled water to reduce Ca2+ and Mg2+ levels to 25 mg/L each in separate trials. This adjustment allowed for the targeted assessment of Mg.ZA’s performance under standardized conditions. The Mg.ZA adsorbent exhibited outstanding performance under these simulated field conditions.

Over the course of five successive treatment cycles, the residual concentrations of calcium and magnesium in the treated water dropped to 1.3 mg/L and 2.0 mg/L, respectively (see Fig. 8; Table 3). This represents a highly effective reduction, underscoring the adsorbent’s capacity for repeated and sustained use. Cumulatively, the Mg.ZA bed was able to adsorb approximately 720 mg of Ca2+ and 670 mg of Mg2+ over four treatment cycles, indicating a substantial retention capacity even with a modest 3 cm bed thickness. The slightly lower adsorption performance of Mg.ZA in real Siwa groundwater compared with synthetic aqueous solutions can be reasonably attributed to competitive ion effects reported in previous zeolite and magnesium-silicate systems.

Prior investigations on zeolite-A and related aluminosilicates have shown that high concentrations of Na⁺ and K⁺ in natural waters partially occupy exchange sites, reducing the availability of surface charge for divalent ion coordination and thereby lowering effective capacity. This phenomenon arises because monovalent cations, although weakly bound, can diffuse rapidly through zeolitic channels and temporarily neutralize negatively charged Si–O–Al and Si–O–Mg sites, slowing the approach of hydrated Ca2+ and Mg2+ species. The resulting competition slightly decreases the slope of the breakthrough curve and shifts the mass-transfer zone toward earlier breakthrough, consistent with the smaller capacities observed for groundwater operation relative to synthetic feeds. Nonetheless, earlier studies also emphasize that zeolitic frameworks exhibit an intrinsic selectivity sequence (Ca2+ > Mg2+ ≫ Na⁺ ≈ K⁺) owing to the higher charge density and smaller hydration shell of the divalent ions92–96. Hence, while co-ions likely compete kinetically for access to exchange sites, thermodynamic preference still favors hardness-ion retention, explaining why Mg.ZA maintained substantial removal efficiency under realistic conditions. The lower overall performance of the column in groundwater therefore reflects ionic-strength and competition effects inherent to multicomponent natural systems rather than any loss of material activity.

sec.p: The recognized realistic purification findings hold profound implications for scaling up groundwater softening in regions like Siwa Oasis. From a technical standpoint, the Mg.ZA bed can be easily adapted for higher capacity applications—either by increasing the bed thickness and column dimensions to accommodate higher ion loads or by extending the number of treatment cycles as modular units. Moreover, system efficiency may be further enhanced through the incorporation of a mixing stage, blending high-hardness input water with softened effluent to stabilize treatment performance and buffer against fluctuations in raw water quality. From a practical and socioeconomic perspective, the demonstrated resilience and efficiency of Mg.ZA underscore its promise as a cost-effective, low-maintenance, and environmentally benign solution for decentralized water treatment. This is particularly valuable in rural or underdeveloped areas where centralized infrastructure is lacking and operational simplicity is a critical advantage.

Additionally, further engineering optimizations could be explored—such as increasing the adsorption bed depth beyond 3 cm or employing a dual-layer column configuration. In the latter case, multiple adsorbent layers could be strategically arranged to sequentially capture ions, thereby enhancing overall retention, extending service life, and minimizing material exhaustion. These design strategies would not only boost the adsorptive capacity but also improve the economic viability and long-term sustainability of the system. Overall, this study affirms the practical viability of Mg.ZA for groundwater softening in challenging environments, with ample potential for optimization and real-world application at scale.

In practical terms, the 3 cm bed column operated at 5 mL/min and pH ≈ 7, giving an EBCT of ~ 1.9 min and treating about 9 L of water within 1,740 min without exhaustion. Model fits (Yoon–Nelson) indicated τ ≈ 1,309.6 min for Ca2+ and 1,154.1 min for Mg2+, defining the typical contact time for efficient removal. Although raw Siwa groundwater is extremely hard (≈ 3,312.6 mg/L as CaCO3), the column results demonstrate that adsorption using Mg.ZA is feasible when operated with adequate bed depth or reduced flow rate, since ion binding is reversible and physisorption-dominated (ΔE < 8 kJ/mol), enabling effective regeneration and multi-cycle reuse.

sec.title: Comparative study
sec.p: As summarized in Table 4, the adsorption performance of the talc-derived magnesium–silicate zeolite (Mg.ZA) was evaluated against a range of natural, modified, and synthetic adsorbents commonly reported for water hardness removal. The results clearly demonstrate that Mg.ZA possesses the highest adsorption capacities for both calcium (268.8 mg/g) and magnesium (206.9 mg/g) ions among all the materials examined.

When compared with other natural and low-cost adsorbents, Mg.ZA’s capacity is 3–5 times greater than that of natural pumice (57.27 mg/g Ca2+, 44.53 mg/g Mg2+) and modified pumice (62.34 mg/g Ca2+, 56.11 mg/g Mg2+). Similarly, it significantly exceeds agricultural and polymeric sorbents such as sugar-cane bagasse (46.1 mg/g Ca2+, 23.5 mg/g Mg2+) and chemically modified cellulose (15.6 mg/g Ca2+, 13.5 mg/g Mg2+). Even among engineered mineral systems, Mg.ZA performs better than kaolin-based geopolymer (76.0 mg/g Ca2+, 40.44 mg/g Mg2+), modified bentonite (68.0 mg/g Ca2+, 12.0 mg/g Mg2+), and TiO₂@Zeolite (131.8 mg/g Ca2+), confirming its superior ion-exchange affinity and site density under similar experimental conditions.

The observed selectivity sequence (Ca2+ > Mg2+) is consistent across aluminosilicate frameworks and is reproduced for Mg.ZA, arising from the smaller hydration radius and higher field strength of Ca2+ ions. This indicates that Mg.ZA retains the structural selectivity characteristic of zeolitic frameworks while offering substantially higher total ion-binding capacity. Furthermore, Mg.ZA exhibits excellent regeneration stability using mild NaCl brine. After five consecutive adsorption–desorption cycles, it maintained approximately 88% of its initial Ca2+ capacity and 86% of its Mg2+ capacity, confirming reversible ion exchange and robust framework integrity. This aligns with its low adsorption energy (ΔE < 8 kJ mol⁻¹) derived from the statistical-physics model, which denotes a physisorption-dominated, multilayer mechanism that facilitates efficient desorption without structural degradation.

From a cost perspective, Mg.ZA benefits from a low-cost, widely available precursor (natural talc) and a simple fusion–hydrothermal synthesis route. Combined with its benign regeneration using standard NaCl solution and long operational life, these factors establish a favorable life-cycle profile compared with commercial zeolites or polymeric ion-exchange resins that require more energy-intensive manufacturing and higher salt consumption. In summary, Mg.ZA surpasses both natural and engineered adsorbents reported in the literature in terms of adsorption capacity, reusability, and economic viability. Its high and balanced Ca2+/Mg2+ uptake, mild regeneration requirements, and cost-effective synthesis make it a robust and sustainable alternative for large-scale water-hardness remediation.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This study addresses the critical issue of water hardness in Egypt’s Siwa Oasis, where groundwater exhibits exceptionally high levels of calcium and magnesium—reaching 609.5 mg/L (Mg2+) and 325.4 mg/L (Ca2+), resulting in a total hardness of approximately 3312.6 mg/L as CaCO3. Such levels far exceed international guidelines and pose serious risks to public health, agricultural productivity, and infrastructure. To mitigate this challenge, a magnesium silicate zeolite (Mg.ZA) derived from low-cost natural talc was investigated for its adsorption performance. Batch experiments showed high adsorption capacities of 268.8 mg/g for Ca2+ and 206.9 mg/g for Mg2+ under optimized conditions (pH 7, 400 min, 0.3 g/L). The adsorption followed pseudo-first-order kinetics and fit well with Langmuir and statistical physics models, confirming monolayer, physisorption-dominated uptake. Fixed-bed column studies, designed to mimic continuous treatment systems, demonstrated the practical applicability of Mg.ZA. A 3 cm bed depth achieved adsorption capacities of 279.6 mg/g (Ca2+) and 227.8 mg/g (Mg2+) with high removal efficiencies. In summary, this study develops a sustainable route for synthesizing magnesium-rich zeolite-A (Mg.ZA) from natural talc via alkali fusion and hydrothermal conversion. The resulting mesoporous zeolite exhibited high selectivity and capacity for Ca2+ and Mg2+ removal and maintained excellent regeneration stability. Field testing with Siwa Oasis groundwater confirmed its practical efficiency for real hard-water treatment. This work demonstrates a low-cost, eco-friendly, and scalable approach for transforming natural minerals into effective adsorbents for sustainable water purification in arid regions.

Although Mg–ZA demonstrated strong performance for hard-water treatment, further optimization is required to support large-scale and long-term application. Key challenges include improving the energy efficiency of the fusion process, enhancing selective removal of both Ca2+ and Mg2+, and maintaining structural and chemical stability during repeated regeneration cycles. In addition, variability in feed-water composition and potential fouling effects must be addressed to ensure consistent performance under practical operating conditions. Future studies should therefore focus on process optimization, material modification to improve ion-exchange selectivity, and comprehensive techno-economic assessments to evaluate scalability, operational feasibility, and long-term sustainability.
